items.title: Gcry 0.35.0: Crystal's own GC, written in pure Crystal, now runs the Crystal compiler itself
items.author: sdogruyol
items.content:
gcry is a garbage collector for Crystal, written entirely in Crystal. Zero C code, replaces Boehm with .

  • Speaks Boehm’s GC_* C ABI, so , spec/std (18,054 examples) and the compiler itself run on gcry as the process GC

  • Parallel mark on by default, marking 31% faster on x86-64, 37% on arm64

  • Two mark workers gained 8-16 points of Boehm’s speed on every GC-heavy workload

  • 48 fixes on the default path, root-complete defaults

The goal: Crystal’s own GC, no Boehm dependency. Getting closer every release.

items.title: Optimal Mersenne Primes Search Using Modular Groups
items.author: jzakiya
items.content:
I just released this paper (extracted from a larger journal article slated for Dec 2026) which uses Crystal code to show how to sequentially generate Mersenne Primes without computing 2^p - 1.

The code is the single core version. I haven’t had a chance yet to do the multi-core parallel version.

As these numbers become humongously large, it would require special software to generate and check 100s of digits values.

It would be nice if there could be some Crystal hooks into such existing software, to be able to write and run complete MPGS searches with it. So if anyone knows how to do that, or feels inspired to try, let me know.

items.title: Generic class new doesn't infer type var for instance var
items.author: 2f1cafc
items.content:
When is defined like this:

class Foo(T)
def initialize(@value : T); end
end

the following works fine as a local var, which matches the description in the Generics section of the spec:

x = Foo.new("hello") # Foo(String).new inferred

However when is an instance variable, it doesn’t work:

class Bar
@x = Foo.new("hello") # compile error: cannot infer type of @x
end

Instead I have to write @x = Foo(String).new("hello") . Is this a bug?

items.title: Accessing Google APIs via Crystal
items.author: nbrandaleone
items.content:
I work with Google Cloud often, and typically use Ruby to interface with the APIs. Ruby is an official SDK of Google Cloud. However, I prefer these days to things in Crystal if possible (it is all about speed!). However, crystal is not an official SDK of Google.

Well, I was able to write a generator that creates crystal shards from the Google Discovery docs (similar to openSDK specs). This is similar to how almost all the official languages are generated these days. The most recent language (Rust) acknowledges this in the README.

items.title: Announcing krikri - An Ansible compatible engine written in Crystal
items.author: weirdbricks
items.content:
I absolutely love Ansible and wanted to see if I could get AI to rewrite it in Crystal and if it could make it faster.

It’s 2 times faster on cold runs than Ansible and about 7 times faster on warm runs. I also compared against Mitogen: 1.3 times faster on cold runs and about 3 times faster on warm runs.

I’ve tested it against thousands of existing Ansible roles from Ansible galaxy to ensure compatibility.

There’s obviously some things that krikri doesn’t support like all the custom Python plugins, inventory plugins and community modules.

items.title: Reaching out to maintainers of downstream Crystal packages
items.author: straight-shoota
items.content:
Thank you for helping to make Crystal available in downstream package repositories. It’s much appreciated.

I’m reaching out to the maintainers of Crystal packages because I’d like to start a conversation about how we could better connect and ask how we could improve the packaging workflow for Crystal. For example, sometimes we need to communicate changes that affect packaging in an upcoming release. We usually mention that in the release notes, and the release pre-announcement published on the Crystal forum.

As a current important notification, the upcoming release 1.22 requires requires 1.14 or higher as bootstrap compiler.

I believe it would be great to have a dedicated space for coordination and collaboration between upstream and downstream projects, as well as between downstreams from different ecosystems. Discussions about packaging are already happening in different places, such as the Crystal forum, random GitHub issues, and other channels. Having a dedicated space would improve exposure and accessibility.

Now the question is how would that look like? What communication tool would you prefer?

My preference would be a dedicated category in the Crystal forum. Most community members are already there, the infrastructure exists. Active participation requires a forum account, but you could passively read and subscribe to RSS feeds.

But I’m open for your suggestions. If you prefer an open mailing list, for example, we could consider that.

Maybe we can borrow established good practices from other communities, so I’m eager to learn about that.

I’m posting this topic in the forum as a starter, but I’m also reaching out directly to known maintainers of Crystal packages which do not have a forum account. I’ll forward any responses from those direct communications.

items.title: CodeGraph support for Crystal — feedback wanted

It extracts modules, classes, structs, enums, lib/fun bindings, macros, accessor macros (getter/property…) and cross-file calls, inheritance and

mixins. It indexes the compiler repo (2,423 files) as well as kemal and lavinmq.

The PR has been waiting for review since July. If you work on Crystal code with an agent, trying the branch and reporting on the PR would help it land.

I’m not affiliated with CodeGraph or its author in any way, beyond having submitted this PR as an outside contributor. Nothing to sell here: I just

want to share what I’ve seen, because I think it can be useful to people

writing Crystal with an agent.

items.title: Milestone: Running an Offline Kemal App with DNF on Fedora Linux! 🎉
items.author: renich
items.content:
We wanted to share an exciting milestone from our work on the ():

Today, we successfully ran a Kemal web application inside a network-isolated container (), after installing Kemal directly as a system library with !

No , no network calls, no , no , no local directory, and no vendored tarballs. Just:

# dnf install crystal crystal-kemal

And in a single script ():

require "kemal"

get "/" do
  "Hello from Fedora Crystal (100% offline)!"
end

Kemal.run

Running immediately compiled, resolved all transitive dependencies (, , ), and served HTTP requests completely offline.

While Fedora’s packaging guidelines permit standalone leaf applications to vendor dependencies (similar to Go and Rust using a ), distributing reusable shard libraries as unbundled system packages has historically been a challenge. Distributing compiled binaries doesn’t work for Crystal because of compile-time macros, generics monomorphization, and whole-program optimizations.

We solved this through three simple mechanisms:

  1. : When building the Fedora compiler RPM, we injected /usr/share/crystal/shards into :
    CRYSTAL_PATH="lib:/usr/share/crystal/shards:/usr/share/crystal/src"
  2. : We package reusable shard libraries as uncompiled source trees into versioned directories (e.g. /usr/share/crystal/shards/kemal-1.14.0/). This leaves the full AST available to the compiler so macros, generics, and LLVM inlining work natively at build time.
  3. The LLVM Primary Symlink Model: To allow single scripts to do while still letting multiple library versions coexist on the system without RPM package collisions:
    • The primary package provides an unversioned symlink:/usr/share/crystal/shards/kemal -> kemal-1.14.0
    • Compatibility packages (like ) live in their own versioned directory without the unversioned symlink.
    • For complex projects with a , our companion tool reads the lockfile and creates local symlinks in pointing directly to system packages—again, completely offline, reproducible, and without touching Git state.

As a bonus during our verification, Crystal 1.21.1’s new concurrency model and multi-threaded fibers ran effortlessly in the same offline container. Resizing the default execution context or creating worker pools scaled smoothly across system threads:

Observed threads: DEFAULT-0, DEFAULT-1, DEFAULT-2, DEFAULT-3

Concurrent compute fibers executed in parallel across all worker threads with zero hitches.

What Does This Mean for the Ecosystem?

  1. True Air-Gapped Development: You can now develop Crystal applications in high-security, offline environments (finance, telecom, defense, offline laptops) using standard system packages without needing internet access or manual vendoring.
  2. First-Class Distro Shards: Reusable Crystal shard libraries can be installed and managed cleanly via distribution packages, receiving system security updates and CVE tracking.
  3. : Anyone can install a library with and immediately write a one-off script using without initializing a whole shard workspace.

Come Join the Fedora Crystal SIG!

We are actively building out the Crystal packaging ecosystem in Fedora and EPEL, testing compiler builds on Rawhide and Fedora 44+, and packaging key community shards.

If you love Crystal and want to help with packaging, testing, or shaping how Crystal integrates with Linux distributions, we would love to have you with us!

Cheers, & (AI pair programmer collaborating with Rénich)

One of the DSLs should have the following structure:

require "horrible/dsl"

We now need to wrap everything following in some blocks (module, class, whatever). So we would need a hook that calls the namespace macro with everything below it as a block. I guess right now, there’s no way to do this.

The next Crystal release, is scheduled for .

As usual, it is precluded by a two-week feature , starting today (). We’re using this time to consolidate the changes and fix bugs.

  • Crystal processes exit immediately when writing to STDOUT or STDERR fails with . This closely resembles the default behaviour of the signal. You can opt out of this behaviour by setting STDOUT.exit_on_broken_pipe = false. (#17335)

items.title: Py-crystal — write Python extension modules in Crystal`
items.author: ralsina
items.content:
First, a disclaimer. I have been the manager in this project, I don’t how it works. Several LLMs have spent a few hundred million tokens writing it :-)

So, I leave you to their announcement

is a framework for writing Python extension modules in Crystal: statically compiled, GC-managed, and expressive — with the ergonomics of PyO3 for Rust and nimpy for Nim. Crystal exceptions become typed Python exceptions, ownership across the two heaps is handled automatically, and the whole C-API plumbing layer is generated at compile time from a small DSL, in either an annotation style or a block style.

A taste — a word counter that Python can iterate, size, compare, and add:

require "pycr"

Pycr.pyclass WordCounter, "demo.WordCounter" do
  pynew def initialize
    @words = [] of String
  end

  pymethod def add(word : String) : Int32
    @words << word
    @words.size
  end

  pyiter def each : Iterator(String)   # for w in wc
    @words.each
  end

  pylen def size : Int32               # len(wc)
    @words.size
  end

  pyadd def plus(other : WordCounter) : WordCounter
    merged = WordCounter.new
    (@words + other.@words).each { |w| merged.add(w) }
    merged
  end
end

from demo import WordCounter

a, b = WordCounter(), WordCounter()
a.add("crystal"); a.add("python")
b.add("static")

assert len(a) == 2
assert [w for w in a] == ["crystal", "python"]
assert (a + b).size == 3
assert a > b                       # rich comparison on word count

class Loud(WordCounter):           # Python subclassing, super() included
    def add(self, word):
        return super().add(word.upper())

Everything is generated at compile time from those signatures: argument conversion with on mismatch, mapped to Python’s , iterators that survive GC cycles mid-stream. And the hard problems of hosting a second runtime inside CPython are solved and tested — foreign Python threads get full access to Crystal’s fiber scheduler through a custom execution context with the GIL released, Boehm’s collector coexists with CPython’s through a serialized collection policy, and ownership across the two heaps is handled by a pin registry plus owned references. The whole thing passes a stress gauntlet and ships as one binary validated against CPython 3.11 through 3.14.

It’s fast, with a real consumer to prove it: wraps the tartrazine highlighter in ~150 lines of DSL and benchmarks 11–12× faster than Pygments on real files (0.8 ms vs 9.1 ms at 300 lines) with , and ~0.1 ms of per-call overhead. The project is MIT-licensed at — a self-contained wheel (Linux x86_64, CPython 3.11–3.14) is on the v0.1.0 release, installable with pip install <that wheel URL>, with CI building and smoke-testing a fresh wheel on every push.

items.title: Alternatives To Snake Case? [ String Splitting, Parsing ]
items.author: LWFlouisa
items.content:
Before I go into the particular error I’m encountering, it’s worth mentioning how I got here: I was trying to make a scripting language in Ruby, because I was originally game developing in that language.

But the syntax began rapidly diverging from Ruby because I’m trying to implement a different syntax besides English, specifically using Francais. This is a whole story onto itself, and more in depth than I have time to go into here.

It is presently split into clemots ( equivalent to keywords or function names in Crystal ), numots ( technically suppose to be quoted strings, but I’m having to use snake case at the moment ), and symbols ( exactly the same as Ruby and Crystal symbols ).

In order to chunk each token, I essentially had to reach a document line by line, then after splitting each line by white space ( what seems to be causing issues in the scripting language, but not interactive mode ) I append each token into an array, and then read each array in a Crystal function. As this is is my first scripting language, I have no idea if this is even the right approach. But I’m presently trying to find alternative forms of terminators in string splitting, because “Hello World” keeps becoming “Hello and then World”.

So I’m trying to replace " " termination with multiple delimiters.

  break_points = [%Q(" ), Q( ), Q( ")]
  tokens       = current_line.split(Regex.delimit(break_points))
  total_tokens = tokens.size.to_i
  token_index  = 0

  ## The actual tokens you'll be parsing.
  parsed_tokens = \[\] of String

Error: undefined method ‘delimit’ for Regex.class

Is anyone encountering that issue?

Presently I’m having to use work arounds by relying on solid_snake_case which isn’t super convenient for long term use.

Note before proposing regex, it’s worth point out this doesn’t necessarily fit my use case and is difficult to understand.

The rest of the scripting language seem to work fine oddly enough. It’s just not structured the way people might be used to, as everything is done in one line.

Yes I’ve tried asking other places, but they kept making my problem worse by “refactoring” into a format that isn’t even understood by myself, whose been at this for over a decade.

items.title: Meridian: a deployment CLI for rootless Podman
items.author: treagod
items.content:
It’s an alpha not because it’s untested, I use it for most of my own apps and services, but because I want some feedback before calling the interface stable.

About Meridian: it’s a deployment CLI inspired by Kamal, built around rootless Podman, Quadlets and Caddy.

The main idea is to keep the deployment model fairly small: connect to a server over SSH, deploy the application, and leave regular Podman containers managed as systemd services behind.

Registries are supported, but optional. I mostly have private apps that I don’t want to push to an external registry, and I also don’t want to maintain my own registry. Images can therefore also be transferred directly over SSH, either as a compressed stream or incrementally through an OCI layout and rsync.

Assets follow a similar idea. For my smaller apps a CDN would be overkill, but I still want fingerprinted assets with proper caching and compression. Meridian can deploy them together with the application and serve them through Caddy!

Web applications use health-checked blue/green deployments through Caddy. Caddy 2.11.2 exposes in-flight request information through , which Meridian uses to wait for draining before removing the old container.

Meridian also supports accessories such as PostgreSQL or Redis, Podman secrets, rollback to the previous web release, logs and exec/run.

I’m also looking into whether Grafito from @ralsina could be a useful way to inspect logs from the systemd journal for services deployed with Meridian.

The alpha label mainly means that configuration and CLI details may still change based on feedback.

Feedback from anyone trying it on a real server would be especially useful.

items.title: Using Macros to make docopt faster. Like, 75x faster
items.author: ralsina
items.content:
Every docopt program carries its own help text, and that text is the parser’s spec. When the program starts, docopt reads the usage section, figures out which words are commands, which are arguments, which options take values, builds a little grammar out of all that, and only then looks at what you actually typed. It’s a great trade for the programmer: you write the help once and get argument parsing for free. But the grammar-building part is real work, and it happens on every single run, even though the help text hasn’t changed since the binary was compiled.

How much work? For tartrazine’s usage text, which has 17 usage lines and 21 options, about 1.6 milliseconds. That sounds like nothing until you notice that tartrazine itself, highlighting a small file, takes about 12 milliseconds total, so the argument parser was eating a sixth of the run before any highlighting happened. Most of it turned out to be the pattern tree comparing nodes by building their string representations over and over, but even with that fixed, parsing a grammar at startup is a strange thing to do when the grammar is a compile-time constant.

The fix is to stop doing it at runtime. Crystal macros can run a program during compilation and paste its output into the source, and the run macro is exactly that. So Docopt.compile(HELP) hands the help text to a small script at build time, that script runs the normal docopt parser, and then serializes the finished pattern tree back out as plain Crystal constructor calls. The compiler sees a literal tree of Required, Either, Option and Argument objects, already fixed up, and embeds it in the binary. At runtime, Docopt.match takes that tree and your ARGV and does only the matching. Nothing new was written for parsing; the same parser that has passed the same tests for years just runs a little earlier than it used to. As a bonus, a broken usage text now fails the build instead of failing on runtime.

The result is that the argument parser essentially disappears from the startup profile: 1.6 milliseconds becomes 0.02. A minimal program that parses arguments and prints one of them went from 3.4 milliseconds to 1.3, and an empty Crystal program is 1.1, so what’s left is the cost of being a process at all.

And this is 100% backwards compatible! I know this sort of optimization is unimportant in 99.99% of the cases but it’s fun. It’s available in version 0.4.0 of ralsina/docopt.cr

items.title: Performance is weird
items.author: ralsina
items.content:
I have a lot of performance data about since it’s a project with a very deterministic output on which I have done extensive performance work, and it’s very easy to benchmark.

I wanted to get a historic perf benchmark for the different releases, which all include static alpine-musl binaries.

The blue lines are benchmarks of each release built on my machine. The red lines are benchmarks of each release using the static binaries from the release (lower is better).

See that performance loss? Static binaries got at one point.

Of course this covers many months in time, so it could be many things:

    After lots of compiling and comparing …

    • In musl, static builds, crystal 1.21.0 than 1.20.1
    • In glibc, dynamic builds, 1.21.0 and 1.20.1

    After debugging, the performance variation can be attributed to … garbage collection.

    • In 1.21.0 + static + musl the heap size is “grow as you go”
    • If I set it to start at 16MB then it’s of all compiler versions I tried
    1.21.0 static build, sqlite3.h → html

    This is a 50% reduction in wall time, entirely from changing a parameter!!!

      While this is probably not universally applicable (do you care about a 40ms startup shave?) it was super fun to figure out!

items.title: Chronicle v0.1.0: Telemetry harvester and context engine for Wayland and AI agents
items.author: renich
items.content:
I’ve tagged the initial v0.1.0 release of , a local, privacy-first telemetry daemon and context correlation engine written in Crystal.

When pair programming with AI agents or conducting weekly engineering retrospectives, human engineers and autonomous agents often lose high-resolution context regarding what was worked on across disparate repositories, terminal tabs, and editor windows. Existing commercial solutions either exfiltrate activity to third-party clouds or lack the correlation depth required by LLMs to reconstruct technical progress.

Chronicle runs as a non-blocking local daemon (via systemd user service) and collects lightweight, local-only telemetry:

  1. : Subscribes directly to Wayland IPC streams. Native drivers currently exist for (), (i3 IPC), and (via ), along with Wayland idle state detection.
  2. : Ingests commands executed across Bash, Zsh, and Fish, mapping them to current working directories.

items.title: Ld64.lld: undefined symbol: close (and memcpy/memset/etc.) linking on macOS 26 (Xcode 26.2 SDK)
items.author: chikega
items.content:
Since updating to macOS 26.6.2 with Xcode 26.2, Crystal fails to link program — even a trivial — with undefined symbol errors for basic libc functions.

crystal --version
Crystal 1.21.0 (2026-07-16)
LLVM: 22.1.8
Default target: aarch64-apple-macosx26.0

sw_vers
ProductVersion: 26.6.2
BuildVersion:   25G83

xcode-select -p
/Applications/Xcode_26.2.app/Contents/Developer

Installed via Homebrew ().

echo 'puts "hello"' > hello.cr
crystal build hello.cr


ld64.lld: error: undefined symbol: close
>>> referenced by mach_o.cr:82 (.../crystal/src/crystal/system/unix/mach_o.cr:82)
>>>               E-xception5858C-allS-tack.o0.o:(symbol *Exception::CallStack::load_debug_info_impl:Nil+0xab8)
>>> referenced 18 more times

ld64.lld: error: too many errors emitted, stopping now
clang: error: linker command failed with exit code 1

Undefined symbols also include , , , and — basically every libc/libunwind symbol the runtime needs, which suggests isn’t resolving at all on this SDK version.

Forcing Apple’s linker instead of fixes it:

crystal build hello.cr --link-flags="-fuse-ld=ld"

Has anyone else hit this on macOS 26? I couldn’t find it reported here or on the GitHub issue tracker yet. Given ’s history of lagging behind new Xcode SDK TAPI () formats (this bit Rust recently too — rust-lang/rust#162928), my guess is the Homebrew formula’s default needs to fall back to system on newer SDKs, or bump its bundled LLVM. Happy to provide more diagnostics if useful.

items.title: [RFC] crinit: Pluggable filesystem-driven template engine for Crystal (upstream crystal init evolution)
items.author: renich
items.content:
Currently, and generate hardcoded skeletons embedded in compiler macros. While fine for getting started, real-world projects invariably require customized scaffolding: domain-segregated layouts, alternative licenses (GPL, Apache, BSD), container recipes, systemd unit files, CI/CD matrices, and static analysis setups (Ameba, Flaw).

To address this, we developed as a prototype and working implementation for an upstream RFC to evolve into a pluggable, filesystem-driven scaffolding engine.

  1. Filesystem Tree Mirroring with Macro Safety:
    • A template is simply a directory containing files, directories, and an optional manifest.
    • Template tokens use double curly braces (, , , , ).
    • Standard Crystal macros (, ) inside generated source code pass through untouched without escaping.
  2. : Templates resolve deterministically with zero configuration:
    • CLI flag:
    • Environment:
    • Workspace: ./.crystal/templates/<name>
    • User directory: $XDG_DATA_HOME/crystal/templates/<name> (Linux/BSD) or OS equivalent
    • System directory: /usr/share/crystal/templates/<name>
    • Built-in fallback: Embedded and skeletons (100% backward-compatible)
  3. Remote Assets with Offline Fallback (ADR-004): Templates can declare static external assets (e.g. CSS/JS libraries or licenses) fetched over HTTPS with SHA-256 integrity validation. A 4-tier pipeline guarantees air-gapped/offline reliability: → → Bundled Template Fallback → .

Reference Examples in Repository

We’ve added three concrete template implementations to :

  • : OptionParser integration, version module, and isolated specs.
  • : Domain layout (, ), Podman Quadlet container files, RPM , and GPLv3 licensing.
  • : Kemal hypermedia web layout with remote asset declarations (Pico CSS, Datastar) and bundled offline fallbacks.

Looking forward to feedback on the resolution order, token conventions, and manifest schema before opening the formal RFC against .
